design_detail: Letter to the editors (Journal of Clinical Psychopharmacology 2008;28(1), printed pp. 114–116; read in the PDF of the journal's whole Letters to the Editors section, printed pp. 101–122, where this letter is PDF pp. 14–16). It counts UK deaths in which ketamine was mentioned, from two sources: the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (np-SAD) database at St George's, University of London, which receives coroners' information on drug-related deaths (July 1997 to December 2006; 18 cases), and the drug-poisoning mortality statistics of the General Register Offices (GROs) for England and Wales and for Scotland, with GRO data for Northern Ireland supplied to np-SAD (January 1993 to December 2006; 5 further cases) (p. 114). A case was a death in which a text search found ketamine written in the coroner's report, or with ketamine mentioned on the death certificate; deaths with ketamine given for medical reasons were excluded (p. 114). Table 1 (p. 115) summarizes the 18 np-SAD cases one characteristic per row (year, sex and age, drug history, prescribed medicines, incident site, recorded causes, drugs found at postmortem, circumstances, verdicts), without linking the rows to individual deaths, and the 5 GRO cases in brief. No denominator, rates or comparison.
can_establish: That at least 23 deaths in the UK in 1993–2006 had ketamine mentioned in a coroner's report notified to np-SAD or on a death certificate in GRO statistics, what was recorded about them (sex, age, other drugs found, recorded causes, circumstances and verdicts), and that ketamine was the only drug found in 4 of them.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused or contributed to these deaths (mention is the case definition; most also had alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, cocaine, MDMA or other drugs, and some died by drowning or a stab wound); the risk of death from ketamine or how it compares with other drugs (no denominator); a trend over time (1 to 4 np-SAD deaths a year, with testing and reporting that may have changed); or that the count is complete (toxicology in about 2 of 3 accidental deaths, and ketamine screened routinely only in some laboratories, p. 116).

sample.recruitment: Registry: np-SAD, which receives coroners' information on drug-related deaths in the UK among people with and without drug dependence; a death enters np-SAD if one or more psychoactive substances were directly implicated, the person had a history of dependence or abuse of psychoactive drugs, or controlled drugs were found at postmortem; the coroners' response rate is estimated at about 90% to 95% (citing the authors' own annual report). Plus GRO drug-poisoning mortality statistics for England and Wales and for Scotland, and GRO data for Northern Ireland (p. 114).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: deaths in which a text search found ketamine written in the coroner's report (other illegal drugs could also be written), or with ketamine mentioned on the death certificate; np-SAD July 1997 to December 2006, GRO January 1993 to December 2006 (p. 114), although Table 1 gives England and Wales 1993–2002, Scotland 1994–2006 and Northern Ireland 1997–2005 (p. 115). Excluded: deaths in which ketamine was present because it had been given for medical reasons (p. 114). The authors state that np-SAD cases were kept out of the count derived from the other records (p. 114); how duplicates were found is not described.
sample.demographics: All 23: 19 male; most aged 25 to 44; 21 recorded in England and Wales (pp. 114, 116). The 18 np-SAD cases: 16 male, 2 female; average age 32.74 years, range 19.8–49.4; drug history (Table 1 row 'Drug abuse history') yes 13, no 2, not known 3; prescribed medicines yes 6 (methadone in 1, diazepam in 2), no 6, not known 6 (Table 1, p. 115). The 5 GRO cases: in England and Wales 2 men and 1 woman aged 20–49; in Scotland a woman of 26; in Northern Ireland a man of 35 (Table 1, p. 115).
sample.selection_effects: Only deaths in which ketamine was tested for, found and written down are counted: postmortem toxicology was done in about 2 of 3 accidental deaths, and ketamine was routinely screened for only in some highly specialized laboratories or on specific request (p. 116), so deaths with undetected ketamine are missing and the count is a minimum. np-SAD's entry criteria favour deaths of people with drug histories, its coverage starts in July 1997, and the GRO periods differ by country. Which deaths are included also depends on who was tested, which may have changed over time.

exposure.measurement: Postmortem toxicology as recorded in coroners' reports (np-SAD) and drugs mentioned on death certificates (GRO), found by text search for ketamine (p. 114). Laboratory methods, specimens and concentrations are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: no concentrations, amounts or patterns of use. A route appears in two of the recorded circumstances (injecting with a partner; snorted while with others) (Table 1, p. 115).
exposure.polysubstance: Common. Ketamine was the only drug found in 4 of the 23 (2 np-SAD, 2 England and Wales GRO); in the others, alcohol (8), opiates/opioids (10), benzodiazepines (7) and cocaine (6) were found with ketamine, by the text (p. 116). Table 1 also lists MDMA or ecstasy, amphetamines including methylamphetamine, GHB, cannabis, ephedrine, codeine, lignocaine and co-proxamol (p. 115). How much each drug contributed is not analysed; the authors ask whether interaction or synergy explains the polydrug deaths (p. 116).

comparison.controls: None: no denominator of people who use ketamine, and no comparison with deaths involving other drugs in the same registers.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history beyond drug history and prescribed medicines, drug concentrations, the timing of use relative to death, and the content of what was taken are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Death as recorded: the cause of death and the coroner's verdict (np-SAD), the death certificate (GRO), and the incident site and circumstances from coroners' information (Table 1, p. 115).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note that a drug recorded as present postmortem did not necessarily contribute directly to the death, that changes in coroners' reporting over time cannot be excluded, and that their definition of a ketamine-related death was as comprehensive as possible (Discussion, p. 116).
outcomes.operationalization: A 'ketamine-related death' is any death with ketamine mentioned in the coroner's report or on the death certificate, whatever the recorded cause.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the records were abstracted by the np-SAD team, to which all the authors belong.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive counts only; no rates, tests or intervals. np-SAD deaths by year: 1999 2, 2000 2, 2001 1, 2002 3, 2003 1, 2004 2, 2005 4, 2006 3; GRO: 3 in England and Wales within 1993–2002 (years not given), 1 in Scotland in 1997, 1 in Northern Ireland in 2001 (Table 1, p. 115). Recorded cause in the 18 np-SAD deaths (editors' count from Table 1): ketamine named in 8 (as the only drug in 1, 'ketamine toxicity'; with other drugs in 7); drug toxicity without the drugs named in 4; another drug named without ketamine in 3 (opiate poisoning, heroin poisoning, cocaine intoxication); drug abuse with bronchial asthma 1; drowning 1; stab wound to the chest 1. Verdicts in the 18: accident or misadventure 11, open 2, suicide 1, and one each of 'dependent abuse of drugs', 'abuse of drugs', 'nondependent abuse of drugs' and 'self-administered overdose of drugs'. Incident site: home or other residence 10, industrial site 1, place of recreation 1, river 1, not known 5. Ketamine alone in 4 of the 23, all with poisoning as the cause and verdicts of accident in 3 and suicide in 1 (p. 116).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable; a descriptive letter. No ethics statement is printed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists each characteristic separately, so causes, drugs, circumstances and verdicts cannot be linked to the same death; the statement that most were aged 25 to 44 and the years of the 3 England and Wales GRO deaths are not shown; the text's count of deaths with cocaine (6) does not match Table 1 (5, editors' count).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Twenty-three UK deaths in 1993–2006 had ketamine mentioned in coroners' or death-certificate records (18 np-SAD, 5 GRO), with 1 to 4 np-SAD deaths a year from 1999 to 2006; 19 were male. Ketamine was the only drug found in 4. Of the 18 np-SAD deaths, the recorded cause named ketamine in 8 (alone in 1), named only other drugs in 3, gave drug toxicity without naming drugs in 4, and was not a poisoning in at least 2 (drowning, stab wound) (editors' count from Table 1). Most deaths involved alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, cocaine, MDMA or other drugs as well.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title calls the 23 deaths 'associated with ketamine misuse'; the text says they mostly occurred in 1999–2006 'with numbers increasing over time' (p. 114); the Discussion calls the series 'the largest available collection of ketamine misuse mortality data' from the UK and elsewhere and says the 4 deaths with ketamine alone somewhat question the high-safety profile suggested elsewhere (p. 116). The case definition is any mention of ketamine, which takes in a drowning, a stab wound and poisonings recorded as due to other drugs; 1 to 4 deaths a year, with testing and reporting that may have changed, cannot show a trend, as the authors partly acknowledge (p. 116); and the letter itself cites 87 ketamine-positive deaths in New York City in 1997–1999, 12 of them non-hospital polydrug intoxications (p. 114), so 'largest' holds only against the 12. The Discussion is otherwise candid that presence is not cause and that ketamine was not routinely screened for (p. 116).

timeline.event: Gill and Stajic: 87 ketamine-positive deaths in New York City in 1997–1999, of which 12 were non-hospital deaths from acute polydrug intoxication and none was caused by ketamine alone (as cited, p. 114; not read).
Breitmeier et al.: 17 accidental autoerotic deaths examined in Hanover in 1978–1997, with ketamine among the compounds found; the letter does not say in how many (as cited, p. 114; not read).
This letter: 23 UK deaths in 1993–2006 with ketamine mentioned, 4 with ketamine as the only drug found.
Corkery et al., Journal of Psychopharmacology: recreational ketamine-related deaths notified to np-SAD, England, 1997–2019 (Tier A list; to be appraised).
Darke et al., Addiction: characteristics and circumstances of deaths related to self-administered ketamine (Tier A list; to be appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: A first count from the authors' own national register; descriptive and not designed to be replicated. The same programme's later analysis to 2019 (Corkery et al., 2021) should supersede this letter for counts once appraised; this card does not use its content.

funding.funder: 'Research was supported by internal funds' (Acknowledgments, p. 116). The General Register Offices for England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland provided mortality data, and two named toxicologists (Guy's and St Thomas' Medical Toxicology Unit; Forensic Toxicology Service, St George's) gave general information on ketamine screening in unexpected deaths (p. 116).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated; the letter has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are with np-SAD, International Centre for Drug Policy, St George's University of London, which holds the database analysed; the first author is also at the School of Pharmacy, University of Hertfordshire (p. 116). The sources cited for the coroners' response rate and for toxicology coverage include the authors' own np-SAD annual report and an earlier paper by the same group (references 2 and 9, p. 116).

what_would_settle_it: A national series in which every unexpected death is screened for ketamine by a standard method, concentrations are recorded, each death is assessed for ketamine's contribution by a rule set in advance, and the counts are related to yearly estimates of how many people use ketamine, so that rates and trends can be compared with those for other drugs.

domains.note: Depends on whether ketamine was tested for (routinely only in some specialized laboratories or on request; toxicology in about 2 of 3 accidental deaths) and on coroners' notifications (estimated 90% to 95%); deaths with undetected ketamine are missing, so 23 is a minimum.

Any mention of ketamine in a coroner's report or on a death certificate, including a drowning, a stab wound and poisonings recorded as due to other drugs; the authors say presence does not imply contribution.
Toxicology as recorded, without methods, specimens or concentrations; some entries are unspecific ('opiate-type, and substance'; 'ecstasy').

domains.domain: Completeness and linkage of case information
domains.note: Table 1 gives each characteristic separately, so causes, drugs, circumstances and verdicts cannot be linked to the same death; circumstances are not known in 6 and the incident site in 5; the 5 GRO cases are described in a line each.
No count of people who use ketamine and no comparison with deaths involving other drugs; statements about change over time rest on 1 to 4 deaths a year.
Limitations are stated plainly, but 'largest available collection', 'numbers increasing over time' and the questioning of ketamine's safety profile go beyond 23 unlinked cases.
Cocaine in 6 deaths in the text but 5 in Table 1; the data periods in the text (1993–2006) differ from those in Table 1; the 25 to 44 age statement cannot be checked.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a description of registry cases (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain. The letter is a short, transparent count from a national register run by the authors and may be cited for the 23 deaths in 1993–2006 with ketamine mentioned, their sex and age, the other drugs found, the recorded causes and verdicts as listed, and the 4 deaths in which ketamine was the only drug found. It may not be cited for the number of deaths caused by ketamine, for a death rate or trend, for ketamine's risk compared with other drugs, or for any combination being especially dangerous. A claim resting only on it stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Background as cited: a self-selected readers' survey of a magazine for clubbers found lifetime ketamine use among respondents rising from 25.5% to 39.8%, and current use from 3.9% to 16.0%, between 1999 and 2003 (the letter calls these UK prevalence figures); Gill and Stajic reviewed 87 ketamine-positive deaths in New York City in 1997–1999, of which only 12 were non-hospital deaths from acute polydrug intoxication, and in none was the fatal intoxication caused by ketamine alone.
key_findings.locator: To the Editors, 1st paragraph (left and middle columns)

key_findings.finding: Sources and case definition: np-SAD data for July 1997 to December 2006, and GRO drug-poisoning statistics for England and Wales and for Scotland with GRO Northern Ireland data, January 1993 to December 2006. np-SAD records a death if a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, the person had a history of dependence or abuse of psychoactive drugs, or controlled drugs were found at postmortem; the coroners' response rate is estimated at about 90% to 95%. A ketamine-related death was one in which a text search found ketamine written in the coroner's report (other illegal drugs could also be written); deaths with ketamine given for medical reasons were excluded.

23 deaths in the UK in 1993–2006 had ketamine mentioned on the death certificate or in the np-SAD coroner's report: 18 notified directly to np-SAD and 5 found in GRO sources; most occurred in 1999–2006, with numbers rising; 19 of the 23 were male and most were aged 25 to 44; 21 were recorded in England and Wales.
key_findings.locator: To the Editors, 3rd paragraph (p. 114, right column, continuing on p. 116, left column)

key_findings.finding: Ketamine was the only drug detected at postmortem in 4 deaths; poisoning was the cause in all 4, and the coroner's verdict was accidental in 3 and suicide in 1. In the remaining deaths, alcohol (8 cases), opiates/opioids (10), benzodiazepines (7) and cocaine (6) were the drugs most often found with ketamine. Most of the 18 np-SAD cases (13) were described as known to be dependent on drugs.
key_findings.locator: To the Editors, 3rd paragraph (continued, p. 116, left column)
key_findings.note: Table 1 lists cocaine in 5 deaths, not 6 (editors' count; reporting issues). The other counts (alcohol 8; opiates/opioids 10, counting co-proxamol; benzodiazepines 7) match Table 1 when the 5 GRO cases are included (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Table 1, the 18 np-SAD deaths: by year 1999 2, 2000 2, 2001 1, 2002 3, 2003 1, 2004 2, 2005 4, 2006 3; 16 male and 2 female, average age 32.74 years, range 19.8–49.4; 'drug abuse history' yes 13, no 2, not known 3; prescribed medicines yes 6 (methadone in 1, diazepam in 2), no 6, not known 6; incident site home or other residence 10, industrial site 1, place of recreation 1, river 1, not known 5.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows Year of death to Incident site

key_findings.finding: Table 1, recorded causes in the 18 np-SAD deaths, editors' grouping: ketamine named in 8 (ketamine toxicity alone in 1; with methadone; with GHB and amphetamine; with morphine; with alcohol; with MDMA; with ecstasy and GHB; and complications of mixed intoxication with alcohol, cannabis, diazepam, MDMA and heroin followed by prolonged unconsciousness); drug toxicity without the drugs named in 4; another drug named without ketamine in 3 (opiate poisoning; heroin poisoning; cerebral and pulmonary edema with cocaine intoxication); drug abuse with bronchial asthma 1; drowning 1; stab wound to the chest 1.

Editors' tallies of the entries naming each drug: alcohol or ethanol 7; an opiate or opioid (morphine or diamorphine, methadone, codeine, heroin, 'opiate-type') 8; MDMA or ecstasy 7; cannabis 5; cocaine 5; a benzodiazepine (diazepam, temazepam or unspecified) 5; amphetamine or methylamphetamine 3; GHB 2; ephedrine 1.

key_findings.finding: Table 1, circumstances: while drinking with others (2); while clubbing with others; injecting with a partner; snorted while with others; collapsed during an illegal rave; drowned; taken before killing himself with a knife; taken with a range of other stimulants before gay sex with a group of new acquaintances; overheated while wearing a rubber body suit; took to excess trying to calm herself down; took a range of drugs over 2 days at various gay venues; not known 6. Verdicts: accident or misadventure 11, open 2, suicide 1, and one each of 'dependent abuse of drugs', 'abuse of drugs', 'nondependent abuse of drugs' and 'self-administered overdose of drugs'.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows Circumstances of death and Verdict

key_findings.finding: Table 1, the 5 GRO cases: England and Wales (ONS data, 1993–2002), 3 deaths of accidental poisoning, 2 men and 1 woman aged 20–49, with ketamine alone in 2 and ketamine with co-proxamol in 1; Scotland (1994–2006), a woman of 26 who died in 1997 of septic shock, a buttock abscess and 'chronic drug abuse', with ketamine, lignocaine, diazepam, temazepam and morphine identified; Northern Ireland (1997–2005), a man of 35 who died in 2001 of aspiration of vomit and poisoning by ketamine, temazepam and alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, row Additional cases from GRO sources (1993–2006)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the authors consider the series the largest available collection of ketamine mortality data from the UK and elsewhere; they say the 4 deaths with ketamine alone somewhat question the high-safety profile suggested elsewhere, while allowing that these deaths may have come from accidents due to misjudged risk linked to ketamine's dissociative effects; and they ask whether a pharmacokinetic interaction or synergy between drugs was the real cause in the polydrug deaths.

Limitations named by the authors: their definition of ketamine-related deaths was as comprehensive as possible; a drug recorded as present postmortem did not necessarily contribute directly to the death; changes in coroners' reporting over time cannot be excluded; postmortem toxicology screens are carried out in only about 2 of 3 accidental deaths in the UK; ketamine is routinely screened for only in some highly specialized laboratories or on specific request. They suggest that coroners and procurators fiscal consider more routine screening for recreational drugs, including ketamine, in unexpected deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says cocaine was found with ketamine in 6 deaths; Table 1 lists cocaine in 5 of the 18 np-SAD drug entries and in none of the 5 GRO cases (editors' count). The other counts in the same sentence (alcohol 8, opiates/opioids 10, benzodiazepines 7) match Table 1 only when the GRO cases are included, and the opioid count only if co-proxamol is counted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small; cite cocaine as 5 in Table 1 or 6 by the text, with the discrepancy noted.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the GRO data as January 1993 to December 2006 and the np-SAD data as July 1997 to December 2006; Table 1 gives England and Wales (ONS) 1993–2002, Scotland 1994–2006 and Northern Ireland 1997–2005, without saying whether these are the periods searched or the years in which cases were found.
reporting_issues.consequence: Coverage differs by source and by year, so the distribution of deaths over 1993–2006 is not comparable from year to year.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists each characteristic of the 18 np-SAD deaths separately, so causes, drugs, circumstances and verdicts cannot be linked to individual deaths. The text's statement that all 4 ketamine-only deaths were poisonings, 3 accidental and 1 suicide, cannot be checked: only one np-SAD cause names ketamine alone, and the 2 England and Wales ketamine-only deaths were accidental poisonings, so, if the text is right, the single np-SAD suicide verdict belongs to one of the 2 np-SAD ketamine-only deaths and the man who killed himself with a knife received another verdict.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ketamine-only figures are the authors' statement and cannot be verified from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter describes the readers' survey figures (lifetime use 25.5% to 39.8%, current use 3.9% to 16.0%, 1999–2003) as UK prevalence, although the same sentence says they come from a self-selected readers' survey of a magazine for clubbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures describe survey respondents, not the UK population; they should not be cited as prevalence.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says that, apart from ketamine, alcohol, chloroform and a propane-butane mixture were found in 17 autoerotic deaths examined in Hanover in 1978–1997, without saying in how many of them ketamine was found.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence cannot be cited as a count of deaths involving ketamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says most of the 23 were aged 25 to 44; Table 1 gives only the np-SAD average (32.74 years) and range (19.8–49.4) and the GRO ages (20–49 for 3; 26; 35).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the age-group statement cannot be checked.
